name: Combs Intermediate School
notes: Seed's 1876 opening is plausible: the Missouri Historical Society genealogy index (from Gretchen Crank's 'Reflections of the Florissant Valley', 1990) lists a 'St. Ferdinand Public School' at Washington St. between St. Jacques and St. Jean — the same block as today's Combs at 300 Rue St. Jean — and a district-history summary states the Florissant School District formed in 1871 and built St. Ferdinand Public School in 1876 (repeated on Grokipedia, an AI source, so year kept at 'probable'). The school's own website does not carry a founding year. Combs is 'famous for cherished artifact, the old St. Ferdinand School bell' (nomoz.org school listing), supporting the site lineage. The village public school was staffed by the Sisters of Loretto from the mid-1850s until 1887, when the public school board declined to license them (Florissant Valley Quarterly, July 2024). The origin of the 'Combs' name and when it was adopted were not found. School still operates as Combs Intermediate (grades 3-5). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Ferguson-Florissant R-II School District (Florissant School District before the 1952 reorganization)".

name: DeSmet School
notes: PARTIALLY UNVERIFIED: seed says 'Known Ferguson-Florissant school built in 1953' and an aggregated district history (Grokipedia, an AI-generated source that cites a district history) states 'DeSmet Elementary School opened in 1953 as the first new facility post-merger.' However, no independent confirmation was found: no 'DeSmet' school appears on current or recent FFSD rosters (2023-24 and 2026-27 district directories), on Wikipedia's list of former FFSD schools, or in the Missouri Historical Society's index of historic Florissant-area schools ('Reflections of the Florissant Valley'). Searches surface only De Smet Jesuit High School in Creve Coeur (unrelated, est. 1967) and DeSmet Public School in Missoula, MT. The school presumably existed (name honors Fr. Pierre DeSmet, ordained at St. Ferdinand in 1827) but has likely been renamed or closed — candidate renames could not be established. Recommend human follow-up: FFSD records center or Florissant Valley Historical Society should confirm the school, its address, and its fate before Track B spends effort on it. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Ferguson-Florissant R-II School District".

name: Brown School
notes: One-room rural school on the north side of Old Jamestown Road east of Douglas Rd (near Carrico Rd), per Ch. 1 of Franzwa's 1977 'History of the Hazelwood School District' as excerpted by the Old Jamestown Association. Founded when 'Uncle Billy' James deeded 3/4 acre to the school board on December 9, 1859; the brick school was originally called James School, then Douglas and James, finally Brown School (named for the adjoining Brown family - David, Clement, William). Taken over by the new Hazelwood School District in 1950, after which the building became a residence/parsonage for Salem Baptist Church across the street (still standing). Seed's '1950s?' close is consistent. The modern namesake successor serving the area is Brown Elementary (3325 Chickory Creek Lane, brn.hazelwoodschools.org - matches seed 'Current Address'); it appears in other seed batches as ALL-092/ALL-120. Not merged per no-silent-merge rule. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Brown rural school district / Hazelwood School District (from 1950)". Track C: the rural Brown School closed at Hazelwood consolidation; its namesake continuation is Brown Elementary (3325 Chickory Creek Lane, still open), minted as ALL-905 after its seed rows were deduped out of the master.

name: Cold Water School
notes: County District #2. A log Cold Water School near Vaile & Old Halls Ferry Rd existed by the 1840s (the school the Brown School pupils were walking miles to, per Franzwa ch. 1); it burned in 1850 and the surviving one-room brick building was built in 1859 (150th anniversary celebrated 2009, per the Hazelwood district press release carried by flovalleynews.com). Annexed into Hazelwood School District February 18, 1950; closed spring 1954 per the St. Louis County landmarks page. Building survives as a museum on the HSD Learning Center grounds at 15875 New Halls Ferry Rd, in front of Hazelwood Central HS. Namesake modern successor: Cold Water Elementary, 1105 Wiethaupt Rd (cws.hazelwoodschools.org - matches seed 'Current Address'); appears in other batches as ALL-093/ALL-119. Building-dating nuance: opened_year left unknown because the school entity predates 1859 (the 1859 date is the surviving building). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Cold Water rural school district / Hazelwood School District (from 1950)". Track C: rural school closed at Hazelwood consolidation (1954); students absorbed into Hazelwood School District elementaries; records to Hazelwood SD.

name: Prigge School / Larimore School
notes: CONFLATED NAME: 'Prigge' and 'Larimore' are not two schools - per Franzwa's 1977 district history (Ch. 6), 'Prigge is the predecessor name for the Larimore district.' The Prigge district elected to join Hazelwood in a special election on July 29, 1951. Franzwa notes at least three 'Prigge'-annotated schoolhouse sites on a 1927 map (named for Charles F. Prigge family), plus a possible 'colored school' on Prigge land whose location is unrecorded. The school line continued as Larimore; the namesake modern successor is Larimore Elementary, 1025 Trampe Lane (63138, lar.hazelwoodschools.org), appearing in other batches as ALL-464/ALL-534. Closed_year 1951 = end of independent-district operation, not necessarily last day classes met in the building. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Prigge (Larimore) rural school district / Hazelwood School District (from 1951)". Track C: the Prigge/Larimore school line continues as Larimore Elementary (1025 Trampe Ln, still open) per seed and district site; minted ALL-464.

name: Hyatt School
notes: County District #10 per a sibling seed row (ALL-254, 'Closed/Converted'). One of the 13 schoolhouses that became the Hazelwood School District (district press release via flovalleynews.com, 2009). Located on/near Shackelford Road; almost certainly named for the Hyatt family whose farms anchored that area - the Joseph Hyatt House (2625 Shackelford Rd, c.1860) is a St. Louis County landmark. Exact annexation/closure year not found; '1951' recorded as probable = end of the district's 1949-1951 annexation window documented in United States v. Hazelwood School District, 392 F. Supp. 1276 (E.D. Mo. 1975). Building may have continued as a Hazelwood district school afterward. No namesake modern school. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Hyatt rural school district / Hazelwood School District". name: Elm Grove School
notes: County District #9; established 1852, one of the earliest school buildings in the county. SEED FLAG: address '450 Brookes Lane' is the relocated-museum site at 450 Brookes Dr, Hazelwood (ZIP 63042, not 63031), not the original school location, which I could not pin down online. A sibling seed row 'Old Elm Grove School' (ALL-249, ZIP 63045, 'Closed/Relocated') is the same school/building. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Elm Grove rural school district / Hazelwood School District". name: Black Jack School
notes: One of the 13 schoolhouses consolidated into Hazelwood School District (1949-1951 window; court stipulation + district press release list). The community's school lot at what is now Black Jack City Hall (4655 Parker Road) was purchased by the local school board in the 1850s; the surviving 1928 school building at that address is now Black Jack City Hall per the St. Louis County historic buildings inventory. Not to be confused with the Salem Lutheran/Parker Road School (1895, private Lutheran school, county landmark) on the same road. ZIP: Black Jack addresses are 63033, not seed's 63031. notes: Seed's 1971 opening confirmed: founded 1971 at 705 Waterford Drive (bounded by St. Catherine and Parker Rd, facing the Florissant Civic Center) to relieve the original McCluer High School (built for 3,300, enrollment 4,500+ by 1971 with split sessions); students split into McCluer North and McCluer High Schools beginning with the 1972-73 year per the McCluer HS history. name: Cross Keys Middle School
notes: Refined seed's '1960s?' to probable 1960s: the Wedgwood subdivision HOA history states FFSD acquired the land on which the Wedgwood and Cross Keys schools were later built during the subdivision's construction (fall 1963 - May 1967); a classmates.com listing shows a Cross Keys alumnus from 1968-69 and a 1971 'The Padlock' yearbook for 'Cross Keys Jr. High' (grades 6-9) exists. The Missouri Historical Society genealogy index lists an earlier 'Cross Keys School' at New Halls Ferry Road just north of Parker Road - a different site ~1 mi south, likely the rural predecessor school the current campus replaced; that lineage is unverified. name: Prigge/Larimore School
notes: Rural one-school district of St. Ferdinand Township named for Charles F. Prigge; at least three schoolhouses carried the Prigge name on a 1927 district map, so a single founding date is not meaningful. Per Gregory Franzwa's History of the Hazelwood School District (1977), quoted at pipes.family: 'Prigge is the predecessor name for the Larimore district, which elected to join the growing Hazelwood School District in a special election on July 29, 1951.' That merger is corroborated by the pretrial stipulation in United States v. Hazelwood School District, 392 F.Supp. 1276 (E.D. Mo. 1975) — the district formed from thirteen rural districts between 1949 and 1951. The seed's 'Closed 1950s?' reflects the district merger, not a school closure: the school continued under Hazelwood and the lineage persists as Larimore Elementary (1025 Trampe Lane, 63138), which is the separate current-school row ALL-464 — recorded here as successor in the modern-entity sense. The exact date the school/district name changed from Prigge to Larimore was not found (Franzwa's book, not digitized, is the likely source). FLAG: duplicate coverage — same entity also appears as ALL-025 and ALL-096 ('Prigge/Larimore School', 63031/63034) and ALL-251 ('Prigge/Larimore School #6', the 1910 county district number). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Prigge/Larimore rural school district (St. Ferdinand Township) / Hazelwood School District (after 1951)". Track C: seed successor ALL-464 is a real missing school - Larimore Elementary (1025 Trampe Ln, still open) is the documented namesake continuation of the Prigge/Larimore school line; dedupe had wrongly folded it into this row. Minted ALL-464 as its own row.

name: Twillman School
notes: Rural school of the Twillman district in St. Ferdinand Township, named for the Twillman(n) family — the John Henry Twillman House (built 1870, St. Louis County landmark) stands across the street at 11840 Bellefontaine Rd and spanishlakemo.org confirms 'the school across the street is named for the family.' The district was one of the thirteen rural districts merged into Hazelwood 1949-1951 (United States v. Hazelwood School District, 392 F.Supp. 1276). Twillman Elementary's own website brands the school 'Roaring To Excellence Since 1927' — used as probable opened_year; seed row ALL-467 ('Twillman School - 1928 Building', in another batch) corroborates a ~1927-28 building on the Bellefontaine Rd site, and ALL-466 'Twillman Schoolhouse' suggests an earlier schoolhouse. The school never closed: it continues as Twillman Elementary (11831 Bellefontaine Rd, 63138), which is the separate current-school row ALL-465 — recorded as successor in the modern-entity sense. The seed's 'Closed 1950s?' reflects the district merger, not a school closure. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Twillman rural school district (St. Ferdinand Township) / Hazelwood School District (after ~1949-51)". Track C: dead-end ALL-465 (seed Twillman Elementary) is the same school as ALL-467 (Twillman School - 1928 Building); repointed.

name: Berkeley High School
notes: Per the Wikipedia Berkeley, Missouri article (sourcing city history): the Berkeley School District formed in 1937 after a dispute over the location of a school for Black students; the new district took over Kinloch High School, which had opened that year, and renamed it Berkeley High School (whites only). A newer campus later opened elsewhere and the original building became Berkeley Middle School. On June 7, 1975 a U.S. district court ordered Ferguson-Florissant to annex the Berkeley and Kinloch districts (effective 1975-76; corroborated by the St. Louis American and the St. Louis County historic-schools survey by Esley Hamilton, stlouisarchitecture.org). The former Berkeley High closed December 2003 due to Lambert-St. Louis International Airport expansion and was replaced by McCluer South-Berkeley High School (ALL-113), which opened January 2004 — direct successor, confirmed. Several campus-variant rows exist in other batches: ALL-378, ALL-379 (Hancock Campus), ALL-380 (Caroline Avenue Campus), ALL-381 (Walter Avenue Campus), plus related ALL-383 Berkeley Middle School and ALL-400 Berkeley School District — all kept separate. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Berkeley School District (1937-1975) / Ferguson-Florissant School District (1975-2003)".

Continuous operation since 1880 in the 1877-80 building (original Ferguson School, renamed Central School 1903; National Register-listed 1984, nomination NPS 84002706). name: Academy of Innovation at Remington
notes: Seed confirmed by district history: opened 1955 at 102 Fee Fee Road as Remington Elementary, built by the Maryland Heights School District (first principal Carroll E. Naves; named for teacher Mabel Brewster Remington, d. 1952). Continued as a Pattonville elementary after the Maryland Heights district merged into Pattonville in 1962. Became Remington Traditional School (K-8 school of choice) in 1982; renamed Academy of Innovation at Remington beginning 2024-25 to reflect a learner-centered model. Still operating — same school lineage throughout, name changes only. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Maryland Heights School District (1955-1962) / Pattonville R-III School District (1962- )".

name: Maryland Heights School
notes: Seed confirmed by Pattonville district history: designed by Joseph Senne, built by Daly for $20,000, dedicated September 1924 at 115 Harding, Maryland Heights — six rooms, four teachers, 140 students. The building became Maryland Heights High School. After voters twice rejected it, the Maryland Heights School District merged into Pattonville in 1962; the district at merger consisted of this high school plus Remington Elementary and Carver Elementary (a segregated Negro school, discontinued at merger). Per district history, Maryland Heights high school students 'began attending Pattonville High School' — hence successor ALL-148; elementary continuity runs through Remington (ALL-151). The 115 Harding building became the Pattonville Administration Building until the Learning Center opened in 1995. A March 1939 'Maryland Hi-Lites' school newsletter exists in the Missouri Historical Society Schools Collection (Box 3) — useful human follow-up for yearbook-era documentation. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Maryland Heights School District (founded as Rural District 24)".

name: Maryland Heights High School - Gymnasium
notes: FACILITY ROW, NOT A SCHOOL: this is the gymnasium of Maryland Heights High School (seed row ALL-163 in another batch) at 115 Harding Ave; no yearbook research should attach to it. District history confirms the gymnasium was built in 1951 for $40,000 and survived as the Pattonville printing facility after the main 1924 school building was demolished in 1998. Under Proposition S, the printing department moved to the renovated Holman Gym B (new Transportation Building/Print Shop completed ~June 2025), and the district states 'the current printing facility will be demolished and used for additional parking at [Pattonville] Heights' — consistent with the seed's 'demolished July 2025,' hence probable rather than confirmed on the exact date. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Maryland Heights School District / Pattonville R-III (after 1962)". Track C: none confirmed - gymnasium/building remnant of Maryland Heights HS; program functions moved within district under Prop S.

name: Penn School
notes: Seed's unknowns resolved by Pattonville's official history: a white-frame Penn School was erected circa 1850 on modern-day Creve Coeur Mill Road on Fee Fee Creek ('at about the same time the Fee Fee School opened' in 1850 — hence probable, not a documented exact year). A new brick Penn building opened in 1924. In 1936 Penn School and Junction School (ALL-169) merged to form Penn-Junction School (ALL-170); the Penn building was torn down. Mabel Brewster Remington (namesake of Remington Elementary) began teaching at Penn School in 1894. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Penn School District (own district)".

Merged with Penn School (ALL-168) in 1936 to form Penn-Junction School (ALL-170). Note the seed's '67' length field is junk (1869-1936 = 67 years is coincidental length arithmetic, not data). name: Penn-Junction School
notes: Created by the 1936 Penn + Junction merger; located on Branneky Lane at McKelvey Road (later called Penn Junction Road). Seed's 'closed 1950' reflects the district annexation — Penn-Junction School District was annexed into Pattonville in May 1950, but the school itself kept operating as Penn-Junction Elementary under Pattonville (still one of five elementaries in 1956) until the 1982 district reorganization closed it effective the 1982-83 school year. The building reopened as the district's POSITIVE School (dropout-prevention program) and the board approved its sale to Grace World Outreach in May 1985. Students after 1982 were rezoned among remaining Pattonville elementaries; no single successor school. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Penn-Junction School District / Pattonville R-III (after 1950)". Track C: confirmed none - students rezoned among remaining Pattonville elementaries after 1982.

name: Mount Pleasant School
notes: Seed's 'closed 1951' reflects the district merger, not the school's end. Pattonville's official history: Mount Pleasant Schoolhouse was established in 1836 by Absolom Link east of the Fee Fee community (near modern Midland and Lindbergh); a new brick building went up in 1884 at 11050 N. Warson Road (the district history also says it 'later opened in 1889 as Mount Pleasant Elementary School,' an internal inconsistency — 1836 founding recorded as probable). The Mount Pleasant district merged with Pattonville in 1951, after which the school ran as Mount Pleasant Elementary until it was one of three schools closed in 1978 for declining enrollment. The building was sold to Christian Academy of Greater St. Louis in 1981. In 1965 Mount Pleasant Elementary was the first school west of the Mississippi to use closed-circuit television for instruction. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Mount Pleasant School District / Pattonville R-III (after 1951)". Track C: confirmed none - Mount Pleasant closed 1978 with students dispersed to remaining Pattonville elementaries.

name: Pattonville Grade School
notes: IDENTITY AMBIGUITY: the 1907 two-room brick 'Pattonville Grade School' at 4020 Fee Fee Road (south of I-70) replaced the 1850 Fee Fee School and was expanded 1925-27; it served grades 1-8 until Pattonville High School opened in 1936, then K-6, and appears as 'Pattonville Grade School' on the district's 1956 elementary list. The district history separately lists 'Pattonville Elementary School (opened 1954)' as one of three schools closed in 1978 and sold in June 1981 — the grade school building 'later became the Vantage Credit Union.' The most coherent reading is that the grade school was renamed/replaced as Pattonville Elementary in ~1954 (which would explain the seed's 'closed 1950s'), but the district source never says so explicitly, so the 1978 closure is recorded as probable. This row may warrant merging with a future 'Pattonville Elementary School' row if another batch produces one. Students dispersed to remaining Pattonville elementaries after 1978. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Fee Fee District No. 16 / School District of Pattonville (after 1930) / Pattonville R-III (after 1951)". Track C: confirmed none - closed 1978, students dispersed to remaining Pattonville elementaries (Parkwood Elementary is the documented replacement for this Fee Fee Road lineage - see ALL-181/ALL-154).

name: Bridgeton Elementary School
notes: Seed's 'closed 1960s' corrected to 1978. District history: Bridgeton Elementary opened in 1953 as a two-story eight-classroom building on 3 acres at 11623 Natural Bridge Road in Bridgeton (two rooms, office and storage added 1956); it was one of three schools closed in 1978 for declining enrollment, and the board approved its sale to the First Korean Presbyterian Church of St. Louis in May 1985. Context: the Bridgeton school district was annexed into Pattonville during the 1949-50 school year — so the 1953 building was constructed under Pattonville; whether an older Bridgeton town-school building served in the interim (the Bridgeton Academy/Moravian School lineage reaches back to 1806) is unresolved and is the likely source of the seed's 'Bridgeton School' alias. Successor: none single; students dispersed to remaining Pattonville elementaries. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Bridgeton School District / Pattonville R-III (after ~1950)". Track C: confirmed none - students dispersed to remaining Pattonville elementaries.

name: Pattonville Grade School
notes: ENTITY RESOLUTION: the seed's 'Pattonville School District - Original District School' (with note that 'the district consisted of one grade school in the early 1930s') resolves to Pattonville Grade School at 4020 Fee Fee Road, the district's sole grade school. Seed's 'Opened: 1930' is actually the district's reorganization year (April 1930 special election converting Fee Fee District No. 16 into the 'School District of Pattonville, St. Louis County'); the school building itself opened in 1907, a two-room brick school replacing the 1850/1880 Fee Fee School across the road. Still operating under the 'Pattonville Grade School' name in the district's 1956 school list. The district's school list separately records 'Pattonville Elementary School (opened 1954)' on Fee Fee Road near St. Charles Rock Road - most likely the same site/lineage rebuilt or renamed, since the grade school was already listed in 1956 and the addresses are effectively the same; treated here as one continuous school that closed in 1978 (declining enrollment; building sold to Raymond Oetting, June 1981). Wikipedia states Pattonville Elementary 'was replaced by Parkwood Elementary starting in the 1967 school year', so students were progressively redistributed; no single successor school_id is recorded (Parkwood Elementary is outside this batch). The 4020 Fee Fee Rd building later became Vantage Credit Union. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Fee Fee District No. 16 / School District of Pattonville". name: Robert Drummond Elementary School
notes: Seed confirmed: opened August 2002 (dedicated Aug 29, 2002), built with Lambert St. Louis International Airport funds as the joint replacement for Carrollton Elementary (ALL-180) and Carrollton Oaks Elementary (ALL-179, other batch), both demolished for the runway expansion. Named for Robert Drummond, Pattonville board member 1972-2002. First principal Jim Schwab had been principal of Carrollton Oaks. Currently operating (drummond.psdr3.org). name: St. Ann School District
historical_names: Historical St. Ann public school district
notes: LIKELY PHANTOM DISTRICT: found no evidence an independent 'St. Ann School District' ever existed. The city of St. Ann was platted by developer Charles Vatterott beginning 1943 and incorporated in 1948 — recent enough that it never formed its own district; it has always been served by the Ritenour School District (which covered much of the area since 1867 and annexed Scudder District territory in 1940 and 1949) and the Pattonville R-3 district. Schools physically in St. Ann included Pattonville's St. Ann Elementary (seed row ALL-174, another batch), Ritenour's DeHart and Iveland elementaries, and the parochial schools. A 1943 Vatterott letter to the Ritenour board proposing a 'St. Ann's Public School' shows Ritenour already being treated as the area's district before the city existed. Recommend retaining only as a search alias; a human could confirm via DESE historical district directories or St. Louis County recorder records that no St. Ann district was ever organized. District lineage (Track C): operated under "St. Ann predecessor district".

name: Normandy Junior High School
notes: Junior-high instruction in Normandy began inside the high school — NHS opened as a combined junior/senior high in 1923, and a junior-high building was added to the high-school campus in 1934 (SHSMO S0326). As a standalone school, the district bought a 30-acre Natural Bridge Road tract from the Sisters of the Cenacle in 1947, began construction in 1948, and the separate junior high opened ~1949 (Wikipedia's building-year list gives 'Normandy Junior High School - 1949'; the school's 'NorJun' newsletter exists for 1960-61 in the SHSMO collection). The same Wikipedia list notes the school later operated as 'Normandy Junior High/Middle (and later 7th-8th Grade Center).' The 'Normandy Junior High' name/building's exact end date is not pinned down online: NSC's current middle school is Normandy Middle School at Lucas Crossing (7837 Natural Bridge Rd; Lucas Crossing complex built 2004 per its school page, which cites the site as the former district administration/Lucas-Hunt property), and NSC reconfigured to a grades 1-8 'EleMiddle' model in 2019-20 (normandysc.org). The NSC Early Learning Center at 7855 Natural Bridge Rd may occupy the old junior-high site — plausible but unverified. Successor recorded as ALL-343 (Normandy Middle School at Lucas Crossing) as the functional continuation of the district's middle grades; interestingly that row's own seed 'Opened' value is 1949, suggesting the seed already treats it as the NJH continuation. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Normandy School District / Normandy Schools Collaborative". Track C: dead-end ALL-343 was a seed duplicate folded into ALL-358 (Normandy Middle School at Lucas Crossing) at dedupe; the school continues as Normandy Middle at the Lucas Crossing complex - repointed.

name: Normandy High School - Eden Seminary Campus
notes: This row is a BUILDING-level row: the school is the same continuous Normandy High School that still operates at 6701 St. Charles Rock Rd. Per the SHSMO Normandy School District Collection finding aid (S0326) and the district's own history page: voters authorized a $200,000 bond to buy the former Eden Theological Seminary property (corner of Lucas & Hunt and St. Charles Rock Rd) in 1922/1924 (sources conflict on bond date); the school opened for the 1923-24 year sharing the campus with Eden students, ~300 students, 13 teachers. Wikipedia's NSC school list gives 'Normandy High School - 1925'; opening year given as 1923 here (first year of operation). A 1949 fire burned most of the ornate four-story seminary building; classes ran split-session 1949-50; the surviving first floor was demolished in 1958 and replaced by Central Hall (completed ~1959). 'Closed 1958' therefore refers only to the original building. The continuing school is tracked separately in batch10 (ALL-328 'Normandy High School'; ALL-329 'Normandy High School - Historical Campus' is probably this same campus) -- flagged as cross-batch overlap, not merged. Actual ZIP is 63133 (Wellston), not 63121. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Normandy School District / Normandy Schools Collaborative".

The district lost accreditation 2013, was dissolved June 30, 2014 and reconstituted as the state-supervised Normandy Schools Collaborative (still its legal name — the Oct 2023 state-board decision 'does not change the name'); provisionally accredited 2017, fully accredited ~2023, and returned to a fully elected local board June 30, 2024. Row retained as the district-level entity; yearbook research should target member schools. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Normandy School District / Normandy Schools Collaborative (State of Missouri-supervised 2014-2024)".

name: Berkeley High School - Hancock Campus
notes: Campus-level row for Berkeley High School's original home at 5924 Hancock Ave, the 'Little Red Schoolhouse' — the building itself is much older than the seed's 1937: it was built in 1902-03 (cornerstone August 1902) as the Kinloch School District No. 5 school for white students, and it housed both elementary AND high-school classes by 1932-1935 (City of Berkeley history page; alumni reunion site). The 1937 date marks the Berkeley identity: the Berkeley School District formed in 1937 amid a segregation dispute (white residents drew the new City of Berkeley's boundaries to exclude Black families), and the district's 'white' Kinloch high school was renamed Berkeley High School (Wikipedia, Berkeley, MO + Kinloch HS articles). END OF HS USE AT HANCOCK UNRESOLVED — deliberately left 'unknown' rather than accepting the seed's 1947: the alumni site is titled 'BHS Reunion 1938-1960', which brackets the Hancock-era HS classes through ~1960 and conflicts with 1947; Wikipedia confirms 'a new Berkeley High School campus opened in a new location' at some later point but gives no date. The building continued as an elementary school afterward (survived the 2011 Good Friday tornado). Successor is the continuing institution Berkeley High School (dataset row ALL-114 — other campus rows ALL-380 Caroline Ave, ALL-381 Walter Ave are in other batches); the institution closed December 2003 (Lambert airport expansion) and was replaced by McCluer South-Berkeley HS (opened January 2004). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Kinloch School District / Berkeley School District".

name: Berkeley High School - Caroline Avenue Campus
notes: Second Berkeley High School campus at 6033 Caroline Ave per the seed. The seed's 1947-1955 window is plausible but not independently pinned down: the BHS alumni reunion site shows the high school 'brand new in 1937' (likely the ALL-379 Hancock building) and a 'Berkeley Junior and Senior High School' photo dated c.1954, and a St. Louis Post-Dispatch school listing (newspapers.com page 139531531) shows 'BERKELEY JUNIOR HIGH 6033 Caroline' while the senior high was at '8710 Walter' — consistent with Caroline serving as the high school until the Walter Ave building opened ~1955, then being reused as Berkeley Junior High and later the 'Caroline Support Center' (56housesleft.com documents it in the airport buyout zone). Possibility not ruled out: the Caroline building itself dates to 1937 (the WPA-funded 'white' high school), which would make the seed's 1947 wrong — unresolved either way. Berkeley alumni report three school buildings were demolished for Lambert airport expansion (the 1937-era high school building, an elementary school, and the newer high school); the Caroline building is likely among them. High-school function moved to the Walter Avenue campus (ALL-381). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Berkeley School District (Ferguson-Florissant R-II after 1975)".

name: Berkeley High School - Walter Avenue Campus
notes: Final Berkeley High School campus at 8710 Walter Ave (a 1992 DOE FUSRAP public-meeting notice confirms the school at this address; schools-us.org directory also lists 'Berkeley Senior High, 8710 Walter Avenue'). Opened ~1955 per seed; an airport-buyout-era inventory (56housesleft.com) described the building as 'over 40 years' old in 1998, consistent with a mid-1950s construction. The Berkeley district was court-annexed into Ferguson-Florissant on June 7, 1975 (US v. State of Missouri, 388 F. Supp. 1058; affirmed 515 F.2d 1365). Classes ended in December 2003 due to Lambert-St. Louis Airport expansion and the school is conventionally listed as closed 2004; students moved to the newly opened McCluer South-Berkeley High School (ALL-382) at 201 Brotherton Lane in Ferguson in January 2004. Alumni report the building was demolished for the airport expansion (barkerreunion.blogspot.com). In 1964 Berkeley voluntarily took in Black students when the Robertson community's high school closed — relevant context for the school's demographics. The school lineage began in 1937 when the new Berkeley district took over the 'white' Kinloch High School building (see ALL-379 Hancock campus, in another batch). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Berkeley School District (1955-1975), Ferguson-Florissant R-II (1975-2004)". Track C: dead-end ALL-382 was a seed duplicate folded into ALL-113 (McCluer South-Berkeley HS) at dedupe; the Walter Avenue campus program continues at the Brotherton Lane McCluer South-Berkeley building - repointed.

District lineage (Track C): operated under "Berkeley School District / Ferguson-Florissant R-II".

name: Airport Elementary School - Historical Campus
notes: Confirmed by the City of Berkeley's own 2023 RFP for converting the building to a community center: 'Airport Elementary School and gymnasium were constructed on this site in 1954 ... The School was closed in 2019 due to declining enrollment, and the City purchased the property in 2023.' Closure was part of the FFSD 'Option 2' reorganization adopted October 10, 2018; the City of Berkeley and residents sued unsuccessfully to block it (STLPR, April 2019). Students were absorbed into the reorganized Berkeley schools — Holman (PreK-2) and the 8300 Frost elementary (3-5) are the probable receivers, but no single successor school is documented. Building conversion to Berkeley Community Center is tracked by seed row ALL-408 (another batch). name: Nuroad School
notes: The all-white school of the 'Nuroad' community — the name of the unincorporated area of northern Kinloch Park (~1930-1937) that incorporated as the city of Berkeley (BHS alumni site documents a 1931 'Directory of Nuroad's Citizens'). A Washington University history text describes Nuroad on April 12, 1937 as a 10-room brick schoolhouse with 300+ white students, one of only two schools in Kinloch District 18 (the other being Dunbar). PROBABLE IDENTIFICATION: the same physical school as the 'Kinloch School' built 1902-03 at 5924 Hancock Ave (St. Louis County Historic Buildings Inventory: 'Kinloch Elementary School, constructed 1902-03, G. E. Reid'), which per John A. Wright's history housed both the white elementary and high school with ~300 students in 1935 — matching Nuroad's size and role; treated as probable, not confirmed. When the Berkeley district was created with the city's incorporation in August 1937, the school/building transferred to it and continued as Berkeley's white school(s) — the lineage leading to ALL-379 (Berkeley High - Hancock Campus). 'Closed' 1937 means ceased as a Kinloch-district school, not that the building stopped operating. Seed's framing (white residents' school ending in 1937) is consistent with the documented split. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Kinloch School District No. 18 (transferred to Berkeley School District in 1937)".

name: Scudder Avenue School
notes: SEED FRAMING APPEARS WRONG: the seed describes Scudder Avenue School as the 'white Kinloch school after Kinloch District 18 formed in 1902' closing in 1937. Per John A. Wright's Kinloch school history (barkerreunion.blogspot.com/p/about-little-red-schoolhouse.html), the truth is nearly opposite: Scudder Avenue was the area's ORIGINAL white school 'built for children of wealthy whites' before 1902; when the new Kinloch district's white school (5924 Hancock) opened in 1903, 'Scudder Avenue School was designated for blacks and becom[ing] the property of the new Kinloch District' — a two-room structure (12'x20' and 14'x20'), eight grades, Black teachers Mamie Lightfoot and Viola Williams, enrollment seldom over 30. The St. Louis Black Heritage Trail site likewise says the Scudder Avenue School became Kinloch's (Black) elementary school in 1902. It was gone by 1937 — a Washington University account says the district then had only two schools, Nuroad and Dunbar — so the real closure is sometime between ~1903 and 1937, most plausibly when Dunbar opened 1913/14; seed's '1937' reflects the Berkeley split, not a documented school closure. POSSIBLY DISTINCT ENTITY: a separate 'Scudder School District' (rows ALL-403/ALL-503 in other batches) still existed independently — Southern School News reports Berkeley district annexed the Scudder School District on August 24 (~1959/1960); it had ~260 students (~75% Black) and no high school. Whether that district operated a school also called 'Scudder' after 1903 is unresolved — human follow-up recommended (St. Louis County school-district records). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Scudder School District (pre-1902) / Kinloch School District No. 18 (1902/03 onward)".

name: Kinloch High School
notes: Kinloch's Black high school — the second Black high school in St. Louis County. The high school program began in 1936 inside Dunbar Elementary (see ALL-394) while the district pursued WPA funding; the dedicated 'black' Kinloch High School building opened in 1937-38 (sources split on the exact year — St. Louis Black Heritage Trail and the seed say 1937, Wikipedia's article text says 1938; infobox 'Founded 1936' refers to the program start). IMPORTANT DISTINCTION: the 'white' high school of Kinloch District 18 was simultaneously renamed Berkeley High School in 1937 when the Berkeley district split off — some sources loosely call that building 'Kinloch High School' too, but it is the ALL-378/379/380 lineage, not this one. Closed 1976 per Wikipedia after the June 7, 1975 federal court order (US v. Missouri, 388 F. Supp. 1058) annexed the Kinloch and Berkeley districts into Ferguson-Florissant effective the 1975-76 school year; ~350 students transferred to McCluer North High School (ALL-032) per Wikipedia. Building later demolished, in part for Lambert Airport expansion. Principals included Orthel T. Roberts (1936-37) and Lucye Belue (1944-74). Alumni include actress Jenifer Lewis and MO Rep. Juanita Head Walton. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Kinloch School District (Ferguson-Florissant R-II at the end, 1975-76)".

name: Vernon School
notes: The area's original Black school: a one-room frame 'schoolhouse built for the children of the servants to the whites in Kinloch' opened 1885 (Wikipedia). The St. Louis Black Heritage Trail adds nuance — it 'closed a few months later', Black children then attended the 1886 Lucas & Hunt school in Normandy, and Vernon 'moved to a number of locations in the area, served black children until the formation of the Kinloch School District in 1902, and its building remained in use as an all-black school in the Ferguson District until it was closed in 1967.' DISTRICT ATTRIBUTION CORRECTION: per that account Vernon was a FERGUSON School District school (consistent with sibling seed rows ALL-427/428/429 which list it under Ferguson), though it served Black children from Kinloch and west Ferguson — seed's 'Kinloch School District' attribution is likely wrong. Remained segregated until closed 1967; students presumably absorbed into integrated Ferguson-Florissant elementaries (the Ferguson and Florissant districts merged in 1952). The 1927 building phase is ALL-397; same school lineage, separate row per no-merge rule. 'W.T. Vernon' is the probable full name (William Tecumseh Vernon, prominent Black educator) — not independently confirmed for this school. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Ferguson School District (serving Black children of Kinloch and west Ferguson); earlier under pre-Kinloch districts". Track C: confirmed none - Vernon School closed 1967; students absorbed into integrated Ferguson-Florissant/Kinloch elementaries; no single successor.

name: Vernon School - 1927 Building
notes: The purpose-built 1927 Vernon School building for Black students of Kinloch and west Ferguson — 'Another Vernon School opened in 1927 to educate the black students of Kinloch and west Ferguson ... remained segregated until it closed in 1967' (Wikipedia's Kinloch article, citing Wright's 'Kinloch: Missouri's First Black City'; St. Louis Black Heritage Trail concurs on the 1927 date and 1967 closure under the Ferguson district). Same school lineage as ALL-396 — this row is the building phase; kept separate per the no-silent-merge rule. Also flagged in the dedup-review file against ALL-428 'Vernon School - Ferguson Campus' (another batch), which is very likely the same school/building under a Ferguson-district label. Building's fate after 1967 not found. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Ferguson School District / Ferguson-Florissant R-II (post-1952)". Track C: confirmed none - the 1927 Vernon building; students absorbed at 1967 integration-era closure.

name: Berkeley School District
notes: Seed confirmed and refined. The Eighth Circuit (515 F.2d 1365) states the Berkeley district was established in 1937 when Kinloch School District No. 18 was split in two, 'Berkeley district being white and the new Kinloch black.' The City of Berkeley incorporated July 30, 1937 with boundaries drawn to include only white families (barkerreunion.blogspot.com, citing John A. Wright Sr.; Wikipedia 'Kinloch High School'); some secondary sources date the completed split to 1938. Per the seed note, the new district took over the white Kinloch High School (Hancock Avenue building), renamed Berkeley High School. The district annexed the Scudder School District on Aug 24, 1960 (Southern School News, Oct 1960) and took in Robertson students when that high school closed in 1964 (Wikipedia 'Berkeley High School (Berkeley, Missouri)'). On June 7, 1975, the U.S. District Court (Judge James H. Meredith) ordered Berkeley and Kinloch annexed to Ferguson-Florissant R-II (388 F. Supp. 1058; SHSMO Kinloch School Desegregation Collection S0707). Member schools incl. Berkeley High School (ALL-114; Hancock, Caroline Ave, and Walter Ave campuses), Hancock School/'Little Red Schoolhouse' (5924 Hancock), Airport Elementary (built 1954, ALL-390), the former Berkeley HS turned Berkeley Middle turned Berkeley Intermediate (8300 Frost Ave), and Holman Elementary (8811 Harold Dr). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Berkeley School District (to 1975); Ferguson-Florissant R-II (after 1975)".

name: Berkeley School District Elementary System
school_type: Public Elementary (district aggregate, not a single school)
notes: PSEUDO-ENTITY FLAG: this row is an aggregate of the Berkeley district's elementary schools, not a real named entity — kept as a search alias per no-delete rule, but Track B should not search it directly. The Berkeley district's elementary-level schools included Hancock School ('Little Red Schoolhouse', 5924 Hancock Ave — the 1902 white Kinloch School building, which housed both elementary and high school students in 1935 per the John A. Wright Sr.-based history at barkerreunion.blogspot.com); Airport Elementary (8429 Airport Rd, built 1954 — ALL-390/ALL-408); and later Berkeley Elementary/Intermediate (8300 Frost Ave, still operating under FFSD) and Holman Elementary (8811 Harold Dr, Berkeley — still operating; may be a post-1975 building, unverified). Whether the Berkeley district operated any all-Black elementary before annexing Scudder (1960) and Robertson (1964) is undetermined — the 1937 split left the Black schools in Kinloch, and Scudder/Robertson brought their own buildings. Reconstructing the full member-school list needs district records not found online; recommend human follow-up with FFSD administrative records or the St. Louis County library history collections. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Berkeley School District (to 1975); Ferguson-Florissant R-II (after 1975)".

name: Kinloch School District
notes: Seed's 1902 formation confirmed: at the 1902 annual spring meeting of the Ferguson School District, white residents of the Kinloch area voted to split and form their own district; a Board of Arbitration appointed by the County Superintendent ordered the creation of 'Kinloch School District No. 5, Township 46, Range 6 East' (barkerreunion.blogspot.com, quoting the ruling via John A. Wright Sr.). The district was renumbered Kinloch School District No. 18 in 1910. Seed's 'from parts of Ferguson and Scudder' is partially verified — the split came from the Ferguson district; the Scudder Avenue School (a pre-existing building) became Kinloch's Black elementary. Segregated per Missouri law: one high school and one elementary for whites, one elementary (Dunbar, est. ~1913-14) for Black children. Split in 1937-38 into the white Berkeley district and the all-Black Kinloch district despite Black residents' opposition; the all-Black district's 'separate but equal' Kinloch High School opened 1938 and ran to ~1976 (Wikipedia 'Kinloch High School'). After the 1971 DOJ suit and Liddell litigation, the U.S. District Court ordered annexation to Ferguson-Florissant on June 7, 1975 (388 F. Supp. 1058); upheld by the Eighth Circuit (515 F.2d 1365). Member schools incl. Kinloch High School (ALL-393/497), Dunbar School (ALL-395, the longest-operated all-Black school, closed 1975), Kinloch Elementary (ALL-508). ZIP corrected from seed's 63134 to 63140 (Kinloch). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Kinloch School District (to 1975); Ferguson-Florissant R-II (after 1975)".

name: Scudder School District
notes: Seed's closure confirmed: the Berkeley School District voted to annex the Scudder School District on August 24, 1960 (Southern School News, October 1960, p. 14 — reducing St. Louis County's regular districts to 28). Scudder then had ~260 pupils, ~75% Black, and no high school; its high-school-age children were tuitioned to Soldan High School in St. Louis. Formation date not found — the 'Fairmont District No. 17' alias suggests a renamed 19th-century township district (seed's '1800s' is plausible but unverified). The district name relates to the Scudder area/avenue near Kinloch Park, but the 'Scudder Avenue School' (ALL-392) belonged to the Ferguson/Kinloch lineage, not necessarily this district — treat as a naming overlap, not a confirmed member school. Member school building(s) undetermined. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Scudder School District (to 1960); Berkeley School District (after 1960)".

name: Ferguson-Florissant School District
historical_names: Ferguson Reorganized School District R II
notes: SEED ERROR: seed gives 1938, but Ferguson-Florissant R-II was created by the October 1951 county reorganization vote that consolidated the Ferguson, Florissant, and St. Ferdinand districts (PRiME Center/SLU; Eighth Circuit 515 F.2d 1365: 'in 1951 Ferguson, Florissant and St. Ferdinand School Districts reorganized'). The merger took effect for the 1952 school year (Living New Deal). Seed's 1938 may conflate the predecessor Ferguson Public School District or the 1939 opening of Ferguson High School. The district annexed Berkeley and Kinloch by federal court order June 7, 1975. Currently operating ~22 schools across 11 municipalities; headquarters 8855 Dunn Rd, Hazelwood (fergflor.org; NCES district 2912010). Yearbooks belong to member schools, not the district. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Ferguson-Florissant R-II".

name: Robertson School District
notes: Probable reconstruction: Robertson was an unincorporated, predominantly Black community west of Lambert Field (post office 1929-1958, roadsidethoughts.com; an early-1800s French settlement that became a historic Black community, per Missouri Sen. Chappelle-Nadal's 2016 history project). When the Robertson high school closed in 1964, 'the Berkeley School District voluntarily provided school bus transportation and welcomed the Robertson students into their system' (Wikipedia 'Berkeley High School (Berkeley, Missouri)'). The district itself appears to have been absorbed into Berkeley around then: Robertson is absent from the 1975 court order (which addressed only Berkeley and Kinloch), yet an FFSD geographical study (studylib.net doc 7845312) places Robertson inside the post-merger district as a discontinuous western piece, and PRiME Center documents that most remaining small districts were annexed in the 1960s. Whether the annexation was formal in 1964 or was only a tuition/transport arrangement that later became a boundary change is unverified — recommend human follow-up with St. Louis County school district boundary records. Operated at least a high school (ALL-410) and an elementary-level school (ALL-411). The community was largely bought out/demolished for the Lambert W-1W runway expansion (1990s-2000s). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Robertson School District (to ~1964); Berkeley School District (1964-1975); Ferguson-Florissant R-II (after 1975)".

name: Robertson High School
notes: Seed's 1964 closure corroborated: 'those circumstances changed in 1964 with the closure of the Robertson, Missouri high school, located in a predominantly African American community... the Berkeley School District voluntarily provided school bus transportation and welcomed the Robertson students into their system' (Wikipedia 'Berkeley High School (Berkeley, Missouri)' — probable, secondary). Consistent with former Robertson residents' accounts that 'our high school closed' amid the community's decline (Missouri Senate history project, 2016). Successor recorded as Berkeley High School (ALL-114, in another batch) since Robertson students were bused there. Opening date, building location, and whether it was a dedicated high school or a program within the Robertson school are all undetermined — nothing found via web search; likely requires county school records or the Kinloch/FFSD archives as a human follow-up. District lineage (Track C): operated under "Robertson School District (to ~1964); students then bused to Berkeley School District".

name: Robertson Elementary School
notes: Diverging from seed's 1964: an FFSD geographical study (studylib.net doc 7845312) states that as a result of the court-ordered desegregation 'all the schools in the Kinloch and Robertson areas were closed and all the Afro-American students who live there are bussed to schools in the northern part of the school district' — implying a Robertson-area school was still operating within the Berkeley district up to the 1975 merger and was closed afterward, with students bused north. Two readings: (a) seed's 1964 marks only the district/HS dissolution while the elementary continued under Berkeley until ~1975 (adopted here as the best-supported path); (b) the elementary also closed in 1964 and Robertson children were bused to Berkeley schools from then — the study's phrasing weighs against this but doesn't exclude it. Exact building/location never identified online; recommend human follow-up with FFSD records or St. Louis County plat/parish records (the community site was largely erased by the airport buyout). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Robertson School District (to ~1964); Berkeley School District (~1964-1975); Ferguson-Florissant R-II (1975)".

name: Ferguson High School
notes: Seed confirmed. Ferguson High School opened in 1939 with 400 students transferred from John M. Vogt High School; built by the Ferguson Public School District on the January Estate ('Blizzard Hill', also the former city dump) at 701 January Ave with WPA assistance (Living New Deal; Wikipedia 'McCluer High School'; the school's own 1948 Crest yearbook history on e-yearbook.com recounts the Ferguson high-school lineage back to 1894). Last graduating class 1962 — students then moved to McCluer High School (ALL-111), which converted from junior high to senior high that year. The January Ave building continued as Ferguson Junior High (ALL-418), now Ferguson Middle School. Yearbook was 'The Crest' — the name inherited from Vogt High School's yearbook (begun 1931). notes: Continuous secondary-school lineage at 701 January Ave: built with WPA assistance and opened 1939 as Ferguson High School (400 students transferred from John M. The rename year is not documented online, but the 'Ferguson Middle School' name is attested by 1989 (a 1989 yearbook 'documenting the school's rebuilding following a fire that swept through the west wing in 1988,' per flovalleynews.com). opened_year therefore records the 1962 conversion of the building to a junior-high/middle entity; the 1939 building opening and the 1962 high-school closure belong to the predecessor rows (Ferguson High School = ALL-416, Ferguson Junior High = ALL-418, both in batch 14). name: Vogt High School
notes: The 1948 Ferguson High 'Crest' yearbook (e-yearbook.com scan) is the primary source: the Community Hall Association donated the site in 1930 and the John M. Vogt High School — the district's first building used strictly for high school students — was erected and named for board member/treasurer John M. Vogt; high school students transferred from Central School. AS&U and STLPR corroborate 'opened in 1930 as a high school with 220 students.' Seed's 'Opened Sept. 9, 1931' likely reflects a dedication date or the Ittner building's 1931 completion date (Wikipedia's W. B. Ittner works list); the first 'Crest' yearbook appeared in 1931. name: Central School - Early Ferguson School
notes: ROW CONFLATES TWO THINGS (flagged, not merged): the Ferguson's first one-room school (opened 1867 at SW corner of Wesley Ave & N. Florissant Rd — the seed's 1867 open / 1880 close refers to this building being replaced) AND the brick 'Ferguson School' at 201 Wesley Ave. Per the 1984 NRHP nomination (NPS 84002706): trustees bought 2.5 acres May 25, 1877; the brick schoolhouse was built 1877-80 (Scharf's 1883 history says erected 1877-78; completion possibly 1880). It hosted a two-year high school course from ~1894-96 and became one of the county's first accredited four-year public high schools in 1903 (NRHP + 1948 Crest yearbook). It was renamed 'Central School' when Vogt High opened — the NRHP gives ~1931-32 via county directories; Wikipedia says 1903; NRHP is the stronger source. Additions 1895, 1904, 1908 (Wilbur T. Trueblood), 1925-27. NRHP-listed 1984. STLPR calls it 'the oldest school in north St. Louis County.' Still operating as Central Primary (K-2) at 201 Wesley Ave. The 1867 building was expanded and moved to 110 S. Clark, where it survives as a residence (NRHP). District lineage (Track C): operated under "Ferguson Public School District (District #3) / Ferguson-Florissant R-II".

name: Vernon School - Ferguson Campus
notes: STLPR (drawing on the Ferguson Historical Society's 'Ferguson: A City and Its People,' 1976, and district historian interviews): the Ferguson school board built Vernon in 1885 for African-American children — a small frame building on a one-acre lot south of the train station (the seed's 'Florissant Road/Farachi Pizza site' area). Grades 1-8; Black high-school students were sent to Douglass High School in Webster Groves. It closed frequently in early years when enrollment fell below the state minimum of 10. In 1927 the district built a NEW brick Vernon School at the western edge of the district for Black students from Ferguson and Kinloch Park. Vernon remained all-Black until it closed in 1967 — 13 years after Brown v. Board — at which point students were absorbed into desegregated Ferguson-Florissant schools; no single successor. IMPORTANT DEDUP FLAG: this is a different school from Kinloch's Vernon School (ALL-396 / ALL-397, batch 13) — the deduped_review_needed file already pairs them; keep separate. name: Elmwood Park School
notes: District's school for African-American children in the Elmwood Park subdivision (Chicago Heights Blvd & Dielman Rd). Began as a rented 'branch school' whose classes started December 4, 1899 (Block 9, Robertson Street); later housed in the Elmwood Park Baptist Church (through May 1912) and the rented 'Fisher place' before the permanent building — funded by the April 15, 1915 bond issue (227-108) — was built starting June 1915 and absorbed the Lackland Avenue School that year. Remained an all-Black school even after district-wide integration began in 1958; an HEW directive forced a plan (implemented ~1974-75) that divided Elmwood students among Wyland, New Overland (ALL-308, another batch) and Iveland (ALL-289) schools and moved the Vo-Prep program into the Elmwood building. 'Closed' recorded as 1975 (last classes under that dispersal; the district history says both the Elmwood building and the original Vo-Prep building were sold in summer 1976 — exact final year could be 1975 or 1976). name: Overland School

The district's fact 14 summarizes the site lineage — 'from 1847 to 1958, the location of the Administrative Center was the site of a school — first the Buck School, which became the Ritenour School, which later became the Overland School, which later became the Old Overland School.' Wyland Elementary opened September 1958 and 'replaced' the old Overland School (narrative: 'the board made plans to sell the old Overland School, which it replaced'); no buyer emerged and the building was remodeled into the Ritenour Administrative Center, which still stands at 2420 Woodson Rd. The seed's 1924 is probably the year the district's high-school classes moved out — the new Ritenour High School opened its own building in fall 1924 (that building is today's Ritenour Middle School, district fact 17). The Overland School building had housed Ritenour's early high school classes since 1914. SUCCESSOR GAP: Wyland Elementary School (opened 1958, still operating) is the documented replacement but has NO row anywhere in the seed dataset — recommend adding it. name: Trinity Catholic High School
notes: SEED ERRORS CORRECTED: seed's opened=1957 and closed=2025 are both wrong. Trinity Catholic High School was established in fall 2003 by the merger of St. Thomas Aquinas-Mercy High School and Rosary High School, on the former Rosary campus at 1720 Redman Rd (the Rosary building opened 1961; 'built in 1959' per the archdiocesan paper's closure article). Closure announced February 2021 after an archdiocesan financial feasibility study; last graduating class was 2021 (end of 2020-21 school year), per St. Louis Review, St. Louis Post-Dispatch (B. Bernhard), and KSDK. It was the last high school in St. Louis County directly administered by the Archdiocese. No successor school — students dispersed to other area Catholic schools. Seed's '1957' likely conflates the building/predecessor lineage: Mercy HS (1948, Sisters of Mercy, University City) merged with St. Thomas Aquinas HS (founded 1954 at Sacred Heart Parish, Florissant; moved to Dunn Rd 1958) in 1985 to form St. Thomas Aquinas-Mercy; that entity merged with Rosary HS (opened 1961, School Sisters of Notre Dame) to create Trinity in 2003. ZIP is 63138 (Spanish Lake), not seed's 63135. For yearbook purposes, predecessor schools (Rosary 'Rosarian', Aquinas, Mercy, Aquinas-Mercy) are distinct institutions with their own series. Track C: confirmed none - Trinity Catholic HS closed 2021; students dispersed to other area Catholic schools.

name: Woodlawn Seminary
district_operator: Private (Prof. Richard H. Pitman; Methodist Episcopal Church, South affiliated)
notes: Seed's 1878 confirmed by the Portrait and Biographical Record of St. Charles, Lincoln and Warren Counties (1895, transcribed on Genealogy Trails): 'In 1878 he erected the Woodlawn Female Seminary building and opened his present seminary, of which he is principal.' Founder Richard H. Pitman previously ran Fairview Seminary (a separate, earlier school on his farm, ~1861-1876), then was president of Howard Female College in Fayette 1876-78 before founding Woodlawn. It reported to the M.E. Church South district conference (1888 Lincoln County history: four teachers, ~50 students, full art/music courses). A Hodge Lodge cornerstone history states 'it continued until 1900' — hence closed ~1900 (probable, single informal source). Consistent with 'for forty years he educated... the girls of Northeast Missouri' across Pitman's career, and with the City of O'Fallon's note that the building was 'the former Woodlawn Seminary' when the Williams family bought it after the 1915 cyclone. No successor entity — a personal/proprietary seminary that simply ended; students dispersed to public and other private schools. Seed's 'classical education for young women' verified (a female seminary), though one biography (Caleb S. Stone) mentions a male alumnus. Seed's 'near Fort Zumwalt Park' location plausible — the site was the old Trevy/Woodlawn property near today's Fort Zumwalt Park; actual ZIP is O'Fallon 63366-era boundary. Track C: confirmed none - proprietary seminary ended ~1900; students dispersed to public and other private schools.
